title: Food waste research project
context: Two students discuss their research project on food waste with their tutor.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Liam, talking to their tutor, Dr Price, about their research project on food waste in the university dining hall. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Come in, both of you. So, how's the food waste project going?

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Pretty well, I think. We've got a lot more data than we expected.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Good. Before we get into it, remind me why you chose this topic. I'd assumed Professor Hanley had suggested it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: He did mention it in a lecture, but we'd already decided by then.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: And it wasn't because there's lots of research on it, either. There's hardly anything on universities specifically.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Right. It was really because we both work part-time in the dining hall, and we couldn't believe how much food we were scraping into the bins every evening.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: That sort of first-hand experience is a good starting point. And how did your first survey go?

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Not that well, to be honest. We actually got over two hundred responses, so the numbers were fine.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And the timing was OK too. We sent it out in the middle of the semester, not during exams.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: The trouble was the wording. We asked how much food people usually leave, and nobody knew if we meant at each meal or across the whole week, so the answers were all over the place.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Ah, yes, that's a classic problem. Now, I see you're planning to weigh the dining hall bins every night.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: We were worried it would take too long, but it's only about ten minutes at the end of each shift.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And the catering manager has already said yes, so permission is fine.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: My concern is a different one. Those bins hold kitchen waste as well as what's left on plates, things like vegetable peelings. So the totals could give you a misleading picture of what students actually throw away.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Oh, we hadn't thought of that. We could ask the kitchen to use a separate bin for their waste.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: That would solve it. So, has anything surprised you so far?

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: We expected Fridays to be the worst, because a lot of people head home for the weekend, but it's actually fairly even across the week.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: What really surprised us was where the waste comes from. It isn't the main dishes at all. Nearly half of it is side dishes, like the rice and chips that come automatically with every meal.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Interesting. Did you look at the self-service salad bar as well?

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Not yet. We haven't got enough data on that to say anything.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: So, what are you going to recommend?

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: We did think about smaller plates, but the research suggests that mainly works in buffets.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: And charging extra for side dishes would just make the dining hall unpopular.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So we're going to suggest that sides stop coming automatically. Students would just ask for one at the counter if they actually want it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Right, let's think about how you'll use each set of data in the final report. Start with the bin weights.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Now that the kitchen waste will be separate, they're the most reliable thing we have, so the whole argument is going to be built on them.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: And the first survey? I know you were disappointed with it.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: We did think about running it again with a bigger group, but more people wouldn't fix the wording.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So we've agreed it isn't going in the report at all.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: What about the photos you took of people's trays?

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: They're really striking, so I wanted them in the main text, but they take up loads of space.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So we'll put them all together at the very end, after the references, and point readers to them when they're relevant.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: And the interviews with the kitchen staff?

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Some of what they told us was quite surprising, like the claim that a third of the bread is thrown away unopened.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: That's a big claim. I wouldn't put it in as it stands.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Fair enough. We'll go through those figures with the catering manager before we write that section.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Finally, there's last year's student report on canteen waste. Will you compare your results with theirs?

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: We'd planned to, but they measured things completely differently, so a direct comparison wouldn't be fair.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: So it will just get a mention in the introduction, to show the problem has been raised before.

lines.speaker: price
lines.text: Sounds sensible. Send me a draft by the end of the month, and we'll talk again then.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: We will. Thanks, Dr Price.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.
